screens.title: Player Input and Movement
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how player input becomes movement in Unity and why choosing the right movement method matters. We'll cover how Unity's Input Manager maps keys, mouse and gamepad controls to virtual axes and buttons, and how to read those values from C#. You will see two common movement approaches: directly changing a Transform for simple motion and using a Rigidbody for physics-aware movement. We'll also make clear why Time. deltaTime and Unity's FixedUpdate exist and when to use them so movement stays smooth across different frame rates. As a concrete example, you'll build a top-down controller that reads Horizontal and Vertical axes, normalizes diagonal movement, and moves the player using a Rigidbody2D so collisions and gravity behave predictably. A frequent misconception is that moving the Transform is always fine — in reality, mixing Transform changes with a Rigidbody will fight the physics engine and cause tunneling or jitter. By the end, you'll understand both the input APIs and the correct patterns to implement reliable movement, and you'll be able to spot and fix common input or physics mistakes in your projects. Ready to bring a character to life?

screens.title: Unity Input Manager and Axis Input
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding Unity's Input Manager is the foundation of responsive controls. The Input Manager lets you define named virtual axes and buttons that map to keys, mouse axes, or gamepad sticks. This abstraction means your movement code can ask for a named axis like "Horizontal" and work with both keyboard and controller without change. In C# you read these values with Input. GetAxis or Input. GetAxisRaw. GetAxis returns a smoothed float between negative one and one, which creates eased movement when a player starts or stops pressing a key or gently nudges a stick. GetAxisRaw returns immediate values of -1, 0, or 1 for snappier input where smoothing would feel floaty. A concrete example: reading Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") will give you a continuous value while holding A or D or moving a stick. A common misconception is that axes are only for analog sticks; in fact, Unity maps keyboard keys to the same axis by assigning positive and negative buttons in the Input Manager. Practical tip: log axis values while testing different devices so you can confirm both smoothing and raw behavior. When designing player movement, choose smoothing deliberately — smoothing helps ease motion but can make tight platformer input feel unresponsive. Ask yourself: does this mechanic need precise instant input, or benefit from eased movement?

keyIdea.title: Virtual axes unify devices
keyIdea.text: Define named axes in the Input Manager and read them with Input.GetAxis or Input.GetAxisRaw to support multiple controllers without changing movement code.

content.html:
Core Concept
Input Manager & Axis Input
Map physical controls to virtual axes so your movement code is device-agnostic.
How to read an axis
// Example: read a horizontal axis
float h = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
float hr = Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal");
// GetAxis is smoothed; GetAxisRaw is immediate (-1,0,1)
Use GetAxis for eased movement and GetAxisRaw for tight, instantaneous control. Log values when testing to see the difference across devices.
Example: Horizontal axis
When the player presses the right key or pushes the stick right, Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") moves toward 1. Releasing eases back to zero. For precise controls, use GetAxisRaw.
Common misconception
Axes are not only analog; they are a mapping layer. Keyboard presses are mapped to axes through positive and negative buttons, so the same code works for keyboard and joystick.
Key Takeaway

Virtual axes let you write one movement routine that works for keyboard and gamepad. Choose smoothing intentionally.

Pro Tip

Use GetAxisRaw when you need immediate responses, like dash or snappy platformer inputs.

screens.title: GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw and Key events
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right input method affects feel and responsiveness. Input. GetAxis smooths values over time, which creates a gentle acceleration and deceleration. This smoothing is useful for camera pans or movement that should feel weighty. Input. GetAxisRaw returns immediate -1, 0, or 1 values with no smoothing, making it ideal for mechanics that require instant reaction, such as tile-based movement or tight platformer controls. For single press detection, use Input. GetKeyDown to trigger an action once when the key is first pressed, Input. GetKey to detect continuous holds, and Input. GetKeyUp for release events. A concrete example: if you want the player to swing a sword once per key press, use GetKeyDown to ensure a single event per press. A common misconception is thinking smoothing always improves feel; smoothing can introduce input lag for actions that rely on split-second timing. To decide, test both modes with your game's pacing. Also verify multi-device input; a controller stick will naturally produce analog values, so smoothing may be useful there while keyboard players may prefer GetAxisRaw to avoid perceived latency. GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw and Key events means use getaxis for smoothed continuous control, getaxisraw for immediate directional input, and getkeydown/getkey/getkeyup for discrete button events.. In practical terms, choose smoothing or immediate input and use key events for discrete actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw & Key events
Pick smoothing for eased motion or raw inputs for instant control. Use key events for single actions.
GetAxis (smoothed)
Returns floats between -1 and 1 with smoothing. Good for analog feel and gradual starts/stops.
GetAxisRaw (immediate)
Returns -1, 0, 1 without smoothing. Use for snappy directional movement.
GetKeyDown / GetKey / GetKeyUp
Detect single presses, holds, and releases for actions such as jump or attack triggers.
Concrete example
For a dash ability, use GetKeyDown so it triggers once per press. For movement input that should accelerate, use GetAxis to gain a smooth feel with gamepad sticks.
Common mistake

Using GetAxis smoothing for precise actions introduces a delay. When precise timing matters, prefer GetAxisRaw or key events.

Key Takeaway

Match smoothing to feel. Test with both keyboard and controller to ensure fairness.

screens.title: Transform.Translate and Time.deltaTime
screens.narratorSegment: Direct Transform movement is simple and sometimes appropriate for non-physical objects or quick prototypes. The common pattern uses transform. Translate with a direction vector multiplied by speed. However, Update runs once per frame, so movement amount per frame depends on frame rate. To normalize movement across frame rates, multiply by Time. deltaTime, which is the elapsed seconds since the last frame. For example, transform. Translate(direction * speed * Time. deltaTime) moves the object at the same units per second regardless of whether the game runs at 30 or 120 frames per second. A concrete example is moving a UI element or a non-colliding background object where physics are not needed. A common misconception is thinking deltaTime is optional; omitting it ties movement to frame rate, so a machine with higher FPS will move objects faster. Another subtle point: when using transform. Translate for character movement, you must also manually handle collisions and interactions, which quickly becomes complex. When collisions or forces are needed, prefer Rigidbody-based movement. Before leaving Transform approaches, test by toggling deltaTime off and observing the difference at varying Application. targetFrameRate values to see the practical impact.

keyIdea.title: Normalize with deltaTime
keyIdea.text: Always multiply Transform movement by Time.deltaTime in Update to keep speed consistent across different frame rates.

content.html:
Process Flow
Transform.Translate + Time.deltaTime
Use this pattern for simple position updates that do not need physics.
Pattern
// Update runs every frame
Vector3 direction = new Vector3(Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal"), Input.GetAxisRaw("Vertical"), 0);
direction.Normalize();
transform.Translate(direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
Multiplying by Time.deltaTime converts per-frame movement into per-second movement, preventing speed changes across different frame rates.
Concrete example
A moving background or non-colliding sprite uses transform.Translate with deltaTime so visual motion stays constant on all machines.
Common mistake
Omitting Time.deltaTime causes speed to scale with FPS. High-FPS machines will move objects faster and break gameplay balance.
Key Takeaway

Transform.Translate is fine for non-physical motion — always use Time.deltaTime to make it frame-rate independent.

screens.title: Rigidbody movement and physics best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When objects need to interact with the world—colliding, responding to gravity, or being pushed by forces—you should use a Rigidbody. A Rigidbody hands movement control to Unity's physics system and allows you to apply velocity or forces in a way that respects collisions. The recommended pattern for consistent physics behavior is to modify Rigidbody properties inside FixedUpdate, which runs at fixed time intervals independent of frame rate. For example, setting rigidbody. velocity = new Vector3(horizontal * moveSpeed, rigidbody. velocity. y, vertical * moveSpeed) directly controls linear motion while preserving vertical velocity if needed. For impulses like jumps, rigidbody. AddForce(direction * force, ForceMode. Impulse) applies an instant force. A common misconception is that you can mix transform. position updates with Rigidbody movement; this fights the physics engine and often results in tunneling through colliders or jitter. If your character requires physics interactions, never teleport it by changing transform. position each frame. Instead, use velocity or AddForce and adjust drag, mass, and collision shapes to tune behavior. Lastly, set Rigidbody body type and gravity appropriately—2D games often set Gravity Scale to zero for top-down controllers while platformers keep gravity enabled.

keyIdea.text: Use Rigidbody methods for physical interactions and run physics updates in FixedUpdate to maintain stable collisions and forces.

content.html:
Definition
Rigidbody Movement
Let the physics engine drive motion so collisions and forces are handled predictably.
Velocity example (3D)
// Inside FixedUpdate
float h = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
float v = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
Vector3 vel = new Vector3(h * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y, v * moveSpeed);
rb.velocity = vel;

// For jump:
// rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
Apply forces for impulses and set velocity for direct physics-driven motion. Tuning mass and drag helps get the feel right.
Concrete example
Top-down characters often use Rigidbody2D.velocity with Gravity Scale set to 0 so collisions still occur while gravity doesn't pull them down.
Common mistake
Moving a Rigidbody by setting transform.position fights the physics engine and causes tunneling or missed collisions.
Key Takeaway

If you need physics interactions, move the Rigidbody inside FixedUpdate using velocity or AddForce instead of changing the Transform directly.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Use GetAxisRaw, normalize direction, and set Rigidbody2D.velocity inside FixedUpdate to achieve consistent, collision-aware top-down movement.

content.html:
Process Flow
PlayerController.cs (Rigidbody2D)
This pattern reads raw input, normalizes, and sets velocity in FixedUpdate for top-down movement.
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f; // Adjust in Inspector
  private Rigidbody2D rb;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent();
    if (rb == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("Rigidbody2D not found on Player. Movement will not work.");
    }
  }

  void FixedUpdate()
  {
    float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal");
    float verticalInput = Input.GetAxisRaw("Vertical");

    Vector2 movement = new Vector2(horizontalInput, verticalInput);
    if (movement.magnitude > 1f)
    {
      movement.Normalize();
    }

    rb.velocity = movement * moveSpeed;
  }
}
Concrete check
Set moveSpeed in the Inspector and confirm motion changes. Remove Normalize to observe faster diagonal speed.
Pro tip
Use Input.GetAxisRaw for responsive digital input and normalize to prevent diagonal speed increase.
Key Takeaway

Caching the Rigidbody and moving it in FixedUpdate produces stable, physics-aware motion suitable for top-down controllers.

screens.title: FixedUpdate vs Update for movement
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding Unity's Update loops is critical for smooth movement. Update runs once per rendered frame and is where you typically read input and run non-physics game logic. FixedUpdate runs at fixed time intervals and is used for physics calculations. When you modify a Rigidbody, do it in FixedUpdate so the physics engine receives consistent, timed updates that keep collisions and forces stable. A concrete example: setting rb. velocity in FixedUpdate will produce consistent motion and reliable collision detection. If you instead set velocity or applied forces in Update, you risk inconsistent physics because Update frequency varies with frame rate. A common debugging scenario is jittery movement after switching from FixedUpdate to Update: this often appears as small positional corrections each frame because the physics solver expects fixed-step changes. Best practice is to read raw input in Update or LateUpdate if needed, store the values, and apply the resulting forces or velocity in FixedUpdate. This separation keeps input responsiveness high while ensuring physics calculations remain deterministic. Process Flow
FixedUpdate vs Update
Keep physics in FixedUpdate and game logic/input in Update for consistency and responsiveness.
Pattern
Read input in Update and cache it. Apply movement or AddForce in FixedUpdate so the physics solver receives fixed-step updates.

Concrete example
If Update runs more frequently than FixedUpdate on a fast machine, applying physics there introduces uneven forces. FixedUpdate keeps the rhythm consistent.
Common misconception
Some expect FixedUpdate to read input directly. Reading input in FixedUpdate can miss frames; instead, read in Update and apply in FixedUpdate.

Separate concerns: input sampling in Update, physics application in FixedUpdate. This prevents jitter and missed collisions.

screens.title: Why mixing Transform and Rigidbody breaks physics
screens.narratorSegment: A common source of bugs is mixing Transform-based movement with a Rigidbody component on the same GameObject. When you set transform. position or call transform. Translate, you are teleporting the object to a new position and bypassing the physics solver. The Rigidbody continues to participate in physics, so the engine tries to reconcile these manual moves with the simulated motion. The result is often jitter, tunneling through colliders, or completely ignored collisions. For example, if you move a character with transform. Translate while it has a Rigidbody, that character can pass through walls because the physics solver did not predict the instant change. The correct approach is consistent: if the object has a Rigidbody and must interact physically, use Rigidbody. velocity or AddForce inside FixedUpdate. If you only need visual movement with no collisions, remove the Rigidbody and use Transform methods. When debugging, temporarily disable scripts that call transform. position and observe whether collisions behave correctly. This check quickly reveals if movement code is fighting the physics engine. Choose one system per object and stick to it to avoid physics conflicts.

screens.title: Common issues and a debugging checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson gives a focused debugging checklist to fix the most common input and movement problems. Start by confirming your input: log Input. GetAxis and Input. GetAxisRaw to ensure the expected values are produced when keys or sticks are used. Next, verify Rigidbody presence: if you intended physics, make sure a Rigidbody or Rigidbody2D and a Collider are present, with the correct body type and gravity settings. Check update loops: physics changes should be in FixedUpdate, while input reads are best in Update. If movement is too fast on diagonals, ensure you normalize the direction vector when magnitude exceeds one. If the player tunnels through colliders or movement is jittery, search for transform. position or transform. Translate calls and replace them with Rigidbody methods. Another frequent issue is forgetting Time. deltaTime in Transform movement. Finally, inspect inspector values like moveSpeed, mass, drag, and collision layers; incorrect values often produce surprising behavior. After each check, make one change at a time and retest. This targeted approach helps you find the single cause rather than applying broad changes that hide the root issue.

Common Issues & Checklist
A stepwise checklist to find and fix movement bugs quickly.

If movement behaves differently on another machine, check for missing deltaTime or frame-dependent logic.

Work methodically: change one thing at a time, test, and restore if needed. This isolates the root cause quickly.

In this lesson you will learn how player input becomes movement in Unity and why choosing the right movement method matters. We'll cover how Unity's Input Manager maps keys, mouse and gamepad controls to virtual axes and buttons, and how to read those values from C#. You will see two common movement approaches: directly changing a Transform for simple motion and using a Rigidbody for physics-aware movement. We'll also make clear why Time. deltaTime and Unity's FixedUpdate exist and when to use them so movement stays smooth across different frame rates. As a concrete example, you'll build a top-down controller that reads Horizontal and Vertical axes, normalizes diagonal movement, and moves the player using a Rigidbody2D so collisions and gravity behave predictably. A frequent misconception is that moving the Transform is always fine — in reality, mixing Transform changes with a Rigidbody will fight the physics engine and cause tunneling or jitter. By the end, you'll understand both the input APIs and the correct patterns to implement reliable movement, and you'll be able to spot and fix common input or physics mistakes in your projects. Ready to bring a character to life?

In this section we make the learning goals explicit so you know exactly what skills you'll practice. First, you'll learn how to capture player input from different devices using Unity's Input Manager. That means mapping physical keys and sticks to virtual axes and reading them reliably in C#. Second, you'll implement direct movement using the Transform component and learn to multiply by Time. deltaTime so motion stays frame-rate independent. Third, you'll apply physics-driven movement by using a Rigidbody, setting velocity or applying forces inside FixedUpdate so collisions and gravity behave correctly. Finally, you'll diagnose common movement bugs—like mixing Transform changes with Rigidbody physics or forgetting to normalize diagonal movement—and fix them. Each objective includes a short task you can verify quickly: reading axis values in the console, moving a sprite with transform. Translate, moving it with Rigidbody2D. velocity, and running a short debugging checklist. These are practical, verifiable skills that map directly to small in-editor tests you can run right away.

This screen explains quick practical checks so you can prove competency. To verify input capture, log Input. GetAxis and Input. GetAxisRaw values across keyboard and gamepad while pressing opposite directions. You should see values move smoothly with GetAxis and snap with GetAxisRaw. For direct Transform movement, run a transform. Translate motion with and without Time. deltaTime and observe speed differences at different frame rates; the test proves why deltaTime normalizes motion. For physics movement, set a Rigidbody2D and apply rb. velocity in FixedUpdate; verify collisions block the player and gravity behaves as expected. For debugging, run an experiment: first move the player with transform. Translate while also having a Rigidbody attached and observe tunneling or jitter, then change the movement to Rigidbody methods and notice the fix. Each check is short and repeatable in-scene, so you can measure results quickly and correct mistakes with targeted changes.

Understanding Unity's Input Manager is the foundation of responsive controls. The Input Manager lets you define named virtual axes and buttons that map to keys, mouse axes, or gamepad sticks. This abstraction means your movement code can ask for a named axis like "Horizontal" and work with both keyboard and controller without change. In C# you read these values with Input. GetAxis or Input. GetAxisRaw. GetAxis returns a smoothed float between negative one and one, which creates eased movement when a player starts or stops pressing a key or gently nudges a stick. GetAxisRaw returns immediate values of -1, 0, or 1 for snappier input where smoothing would feel floaty. A concrete example: reading Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") will give you a continuous value while holding A or D or moving a stick. A common misconception is that axes are only for analog sticks; in fact, Unity maps keyboard keys to the same axis by assigning positive and negative buttons in the Input Manager. Practical tip: log axis values while testing different devices so you can confirm both smoothing and raw behavior. When designing player movement, choose smoothing deliberately — smoothing helps ease motion but can make tight platformer input feel unresponsive. Ask yourself: does this mechanic need precise instant input, or benefit from eased movement?

Choosing the right input method affects feel and responsiveness. Input. GetAxis smooths values over time, which creates a gentle acceleration and deceleration. This smoothing is useful for camera pans or movement that should feel weighty. Input. GetAxisRaw returns immediate -1, 0, or 1 values with no smoothing, making it ideal for mechanics that require instant reaction, such as tile-based movement or tight platformer controls. For single press detection, use Input. GetKeyDown to trigger an action once when the key is first pressed, Input. GetKey to detect continuous holds, and Input. GetKeyUp for release events. A concrete example: if you want the player to swing a sword once per key press, use GetKeyDown to ensure a single event per press. A common misconception is thinking smoothing always improves feel; smoothing can introduce input lag for actions that rely on split-second timing. To decide, test both modes with your game's pacing. Also verify multi-device input; a controller stick will naturally produce analog values, so smoothing may be useful there while keyboard players may prefer GetAxisRaw to avoid perceived latency. In practical terms, choose smoothing or immediate input and use key events for discrete actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Direct Transform movement is simple and sometimes appropriate for non-physical objects or quick prototypes. The common pattern uses transform. Translate with a direction vector multiplied by speed. However, Update runs once per frame, so movement amount per frame depends on frame rate. To normalize movement across frame rates, multiply by Time. deltaTime, which is the elapsed seconds since the last frame. For example, transform. Translate(direction * speed * Time. deltaTime) moves the object at the same units per second regardless of whether the game runs at 30 or 120 frames per second. A concrete example is moving a UI element or a non-colliding background object where physics are not needed. A common misconception is thinking deltaTime is optional; omitting it ties movement to frame rate, so a machine with higher FPS will move objects faster. Another subtle point: when using transform. When objects need to interact with the world—colliding, responding to gravity, or being pushed by forces—you should use a Rigidbody. A Rigidbody hands movement control to Unity's physics system and allows you to apply velocity or forces in a way that respects collisions. The recommended pattern for consistent physics behavior is to modify Rigidbody properties inside FixedUpdate, which runs at fixed time intervals independent of frame rate. For example, setting rigidbody. velocity = new Vector3(horizontal * moveSpeed, rigidbody. velocity. y, vertical * moveSpeed) directly controls linear motion while preserving vertical velocity if needed. Instead, use velocity or AddForce and adjust drag, mass, and collision shapes to tune behavior.
